newsitem.title: GERMANY: Buba's Welteke-sees no need to alter rates soon.
newsitem.headline: Buba's Welteke-sees no need to alter rates soon.

text.p: Germany's Bundesbank is likely to leave key interest rates steady for some time as there are currently no pressing reasons to alter policies, a council member said on Tuesday.

"The arguments for a rate change in either direction would more or less cancel each other out for a longer period of time. So we have no reason to think about whether we should change interest rates or not," council member Ernst Welteke told Reuters in an interview.
The Bundesbank last lowered its discount and Lombard rates to 2.50 and 4.50 percent respectively in April 1996 and has kept the main money market rate fixed at three percent since August.

Some independent economists even predicted the Bundesbank would never again alter policies before handing over its policy-making reins to the European Central Bank after currency union is scheduled to begin in 1999.

But in light of Germany's stubbornly high unemployment levels, topping four million people, critics have called on the Bundesbank to cut interest rates once again, especially as there are no acute dangers on the inflation front.
The fiercely independent Bundesbank however has brushed off these demands which have been made repeatedly each month when another very high jobless number is released.
"We have the impression that monetary policy has done its part and that liquidity conditions in the German economy are sufficient to finance stronger growth," Welteke argued.
Instead the labour market needs structural reforms to help curb the jobless rate, Welteke added.

While Welteke, who is also president of the state central bank in Hesse, agreed with government predictions that economic growth would reach 2.5 percent this year but that this would be insufficient to significantly pared back the jobless rate.
"In light of the numbers we have, one can consider that we can reach real growth of 2.5 percent but this will not be enough to create a marked improvement on the labour market," Welteke said.
With inflation running at well under two percent, the Bundesbank's traditional medium-term goal, Welteke also said there were no worries about prices pressures.
"When you look at the import of export prices, there continue to be no worries about the issue," Welteke said.

Turning to M3 money supply, another key policy indicator, Welteke said developments were improving and that he was confident growth would retreat into the Bundesbank's self-set target corridor this year.
"M3 is moving towards the direction of the corridor and there is the well-founded hope that the data will soon be in the corridor," Welteke said.
The May data are expected to be released at the end of this week or early next week.

The Bundesbank never gives an exact release date, arguing it could better serve the market by releasing the information precisely when it becomes available rather than holding it for a time in order to meet a previously agreed to release date.
Last December the Bundesbank set its 1997 target corridor between 3.5 and 6.5 percent and in April M3 stood at 6.7 percent.

As part of the Bundesbank's efforts to keep interest rate speculation in check, Welteke also said that the Bundesbank was not currently considering returning to a variable rate tender for its weekly securities repurchase operations.
"We face a lot of interest rate expectations in the markets, and since we do not want to create expectations of a change, why should be switch back to a variable rate repo," Welteke said.
